Zeros and Nines

Place ValueCountingArithmetic
Game: Write a number and its multiples in a table, then look for a 0 or a 9 in one column.
How to play: Click the right or left half of a blue digit to change it, then press Check column. You can also use the arrow keys.
Look for the math

Write any number S, then its multiples 2S, 3S and so on underneath. The columns look messy, yet something always turns up. Try editing the blue digits and checking a column for yourself.

Reading the table

The blue top row is S. Beneath it are 2S through base × S, all written in the chosen positional system. Bases above ten use A for 10, B for 11 and so on. Columns are counted from the right: the units column is column 0, the tens column is column 1. Where a multiple is too short to reach a column, we fill the gap with a 0, just as the puzzle suggests.

Why a 0 or a 9 must appear

Among the ten rows S, 2S, …, 10S, suppose no digit in a column is 0 or 9. Only the eight digits 1 through 8 are left, so two rows must have the same digit there: this is the pigeonhole principle. Say they are aS and bS with a > b. Their difference (a − b)S is one of the rows in the table, because a − b lies between 1 and 9. In that column, aS − bS gives 0 when nothing is borrowed from the column to the right, and 9 when something is borrowed. Either way a 0 or a 9 is there after all.

Where the warning goes wrong

The page warns that for S = 1050 through 1089 (and 2050 through 2089, and so on) the hundreds column has neither 0 nor 9. That is true of the nine multiples 2S through 10S: for 1050 their hundreds digits are 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5. It stops being true once the blue S row is included: S itself has a 0 there. The proof needs that row, since the matching pair can differ by 1. The logic test checked every column of S, 2S, …, 10S for all S up to 20,000 in base 10, and up to 150 in every base from 3 to 36; in base r the guaranteed pair is 0 or r − 1. It also checked that all 1,600 hundreds-column exceptions below 20,000 are rescued by the S row.

Set the base to 3 and check a column: which two digits must appear? Then try S = 1050 and compare the hundreds column with and without the blue row.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
